impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent holder's conditioning of patent licenses on customers' exclusive purchase of unpatented products constitutes unlawful tying under the Sherman Act, and whether the defense that the tied products are 'nonstaple goods' lacking substantial non-infringing uses shields the patent holder from antitrust liability.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the jury's finding that Ingevity engaged in unlawful tying by conditioning licenses to its fuel vapor canister patent on customers' agreements to exclusively purchase Ingevity's unpatented carbon honeycomb products. The court upheld the antitrust damages award, rejecting Ingevity's argument that its honeycombs were nonstaple goods protected from antitrust liability under patent law.
impacts.positiveImplications: Competitors of patent holders who engage in tying arrangements have a clear path to antitrust recovery. The decision reinforces that antitrust law constrains patent licensing practices that extend monopoly power beyond the patent's scope.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders who bundle patent licenses with exclusive purchasing requirements for unpatented products face significant antitrust liability risk, even when the tied products are related to the patented technology. Companies must carefully structure patent licensing programs to avoid tying claims.

impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting judgment as a matter of law that Teva's headache patents claiming methods of treating headache using humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies were invalid for failure to satisfy both the written-description and enablement requirements of 35 U.S.C. § 112.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's JMOL of invalidity of Teva's headache patents, which claim methods of using humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies to treat headache. The case involves Teva's Ajovy product and Lilly's competing migraine treatment. The reversal reinstates the jury's findings of willful infringement and validity, potentially worth substantial damages in the multi-billion-dollar migraine treatment market.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders in the pharmaceutical/biologics space benefit from a more favorable standard for written description and enablement of genus claims where the specification discloses known methods and at least one species. This supports broader patent protection for biologic drug classes.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic and biosimilar developers face broader patent barriers when pioneer patentees can claim genus-level methods using known antibody classes with limited specific disclosure. This may extend exclusivity periods and delay competition.

impacts.caseName: Trustees of Columbia University v. Gen Digital Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to detecting anomalous program executions by emulating program behavior and comparing function calls to a model are directed to an abstract idea under Alice step one, and whether the district court erred in allowing damages based on foreign sales of Norton antivirus software.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated a $185 million jury verdict for Columbia, holding that patents claiming methods for detecting anomalous program executions (used in Norton antivirus software) are abstract at Alice step one and require further proceedings on step two. The court also held the district court erred in allowing damages based on Norton's foreign sales, establishing important limits on extraterritorial patent damages.
impacts.positiveImplications: Technology companies accused of infringing software patents benefit from the court's application of Alice to cybersecurity detection methods. The ruling on foreign sales limits plaintiffs' ability to recover damages based on overseas revenue.
impacts.negativeImplications: University and research institution patent holders face heightened risk that software-implemented security and detection patents will be found abstract under § 101. Patentees also lose the ability to recover damages tied to foreign sales of accused products.

impacts.caseName: GoTV Streaming, LLC v. Netflix, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to a server that tailors content delivery specifications to a wireless device's screen size or capabilities are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that GoTV's streaming media patents claiming server-side tailoring of content to a device's capabilities are ineligible for patenting under § 101, reversing a $2.5 million jury verdict in favor of GoTV against Netflix. The court found the claims directed to the abstract idea of adapting content presentation to device characteristics.
impacts.positiveImplications: Streaming platforms and content delivery companies benefit from the invalidation of broad patents covering adaptive content delivery, reducing litigation exposure in the streaming media space.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders with claims directed to server-side content optimization and adaptive streaming face significant eligibility challenges. The ruling narrows the scope of enforceable patents in the digital content delivery industry.

impacts.caseName: Global Tubing LLC v. Tenaris Coiled Tubes LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether summary judgment was properly granted on inequitable conduct in obtaining coiled tubing patents and on a Walker Process antitrust fraud claim alleging attempted monopolization through enforcement of fraudulently obtained patents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated summary judgment on both Tenaris's inequitable conduct defense and Global Tubing's Walker Process antitrust fraud claim, finding genuine disputes of material fact on both issues. The case involves whether Tenaris withheld known prior art (the CYMAX product) during patent prosecution and whether this rose to the level of fraud supporting antitrust liability for attempted monopolization.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies facing patent assertions have a viable path to challenge patents through inequitable conduct and pursue antitrust counterclaims under Walker Process where the patentee knowingly withheld material prior art during prosecution.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face combined exposure to both patent unenforceability and antitrust damages if they fail to disclose material prior art during prosecution. The intersection of patent fraud and antitrust liability creates significant litigation risk.

impacts.caseName: VLSI Technology LLC v. Intel Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting summary judgment of noninfringement of a multi-core processor patent based on extraterritoriality and in rejecting VLSI's doctrine of equivalents theory.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed in part the district court's grant of summary judgment of noninfringement to Intel, finding that VLSI raised genuine issues of material fact regarding its doctrine of equivalents theory for a multi-core processor patent. The court affirmed on extraterritoriality grounds for certain claims but remanded for further proceedings on equivalents.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders asserting semiconductor and processor patents retain the ability to pursue infringement under the doctrine of equivalents even where literal infringement may not be established, preserving broader patent enforcement tools.
impacts.negativeImplications: Semiconductor companies face continued exposure to patent claims under the doctrine of equivalents even when they design around literal claim limitations. The extraterritoriality ruling, however, provides some protection for foreign manufacturing operations.

impacts.caseName: Apple Inc. v. International Trade Commission
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the ITC correctly found that Apple Watch models with blood oxygen measurement functionality infringed Masimo's patents covering wearable blood oxygen measurement devices, and whether Masimo satisfied the domestic industry requirement.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the ITC's finding that Apple violated Section 337 of the Tariff Act by importing and selling Apple Watch models that infringed Masimo's patents for wearable blood oxygen measurement technology. The court upheld the limited exclusion order barring importation of infringing Apple Watch models, affirming validity, infringement, and domestic industry findings.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders with domestic manufacturing or R&D operations can effectively use ITC exclusion orders to bar importation of competing products, providing powerful leverage against large technology companies with foreign manufacturing.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies that integrate patented health-monitoring features into consumer electronics face the risk of import bans through ITC proceedings, potentially requiring costly design-arounds or licensing arrangements to maintain market access.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Rule 30(b)(6) corporate representative testimony based on corporate knowledge (rather than personal knowledge) is admissible at summary judgment to establish pre-critical-date sales for the on-sale bar under 35 U.S.C. § 102(b), and whether source code constitutes hearsay.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment invalidating engine controller reprogramming patents under the on-sale bar, holding that Rule 30(b)(6) testimony from a corporate representative is admissible even when the witness lacks personal knowledge of the events, and that computer source code is not hearsay because it consists of machine commands rather than human statements.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers can rely on corporate representative testimony and source code evidence to prove prior art sales, even when no witnesses with personal knowledge remain available. This strengthens invalidity defenses based on historical commercial activity.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face an expanded evidentiary landscape for on-sale bar challenges. The admissibility of 30(b)(6) testimony without personal knowledge and source code as non-hearsay makes it easier for defendants to prove prior commercial sales invalidating patents.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court abused its discretion in excluding a patent plaintiff's damages expert report and granting summary judgment based on absence of a remedy.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's exclusion of Exafer's damages expert report in a patent infringement case against Microsoft's Azure platform, finding the exclusion was improper. The court vacated summary judgment that had been entered against Exafer solely because, with the expert excluded, Exafer could not establish any damages remedy.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent plaintiffs benefit from a more permissive standard for admissibility of damages expert testimony, ensuring that technical disputes about damages methodology are resolved at trial rather than on Daubert motions.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies defending patent cases face reduced ability to defeat infringement claims through exclusion of opposing damages experts. Cases are more likely to proceed to trial on damages questions.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform constellations for digital communication systems are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL of non-infringement and no damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit issued a mixed ruling in this patent case involving digital communication standard technology, vacating summary judgment of eligibility for certain patent claims while affirming eligibility for others and affirming the denial of JMOL on infringement and damages. The case involves patents essential to broadcast communication standards used in LG televisions.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders whose claims are tied to specific technical implementations in communication standards may maintain eligibility, and the affirmance of damages provides certainty for standard-essential patent licensing.
impacts.negativeImplications: Electronics manufacturers implementing communication standards remain exposed to significant patent damages. The partial vacatur on eligibility creates uncertainty about the patent-eligibility of optimization-based communication technology patents.

impacts.caseName: National Veterans Legal Services Program v. United States
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly approved a $125 million class action settlement resolving claims that the federal judiciary overcharged PACER users by using fees to fund projects unrelated to PACER operations, and whether incentive awards to class representatives were permissible.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed approval of a $125 million nationwide class action settlement in which the government agreed to reimburse PACER users who were overcharged for court record access fees. The court upheld the settlement, attorneys' fees, and incentive awards to nonprofit class representatives, rejecting objections that the district court lacked jurisdiction and that incentive awards were impermissible.
impacts.positiveImplications: The decision validates class settlement structures involving incentive awards to organizational class representatives and confirms the viability of Little Tucker Act class claims against the government for overcharges.

impacts.caseName: Ascendis Pharma A/S v. BioMarin Pharmaceutical Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a respondent in an ITC proceeding may obtain a mandatory stay under 28 U.S.C. § 1659(a)(2) of a refiled declaratory judgment action when it missed the deadline to seek a stay in the original action involving the same parties and issues.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that an ITC respondent cannot circumvent the statutory deadline for obtaining a mandatory stay of a parallel district court action by dismissing and refiling the declaratory judgment action. BioMarin had missed the 30-day deadline to seek a stay in Ascendis's original DJ action and attempted to obtain a stay by having Ascendis refile. The court rejected this gamesmanship.
impacts.positiveImplications: Pharmaceutical and life sciences companies filing declaratory judgment actions can proceed with district court litigation without being subject to mandatory stays when the ITC respondent has missed the statutory deadline, preserving timely access to judicial resolution of patent disputes.
impacts.negativeImplications: ITC respondents who miss the 30-day deadline to seek a mandatory stay of parallel district court proceedings cannot cure the missed deadline through procedural maneuvers such as refiling, potentially forcing them to litigate on two fronts simultaneously.

impacts.caseName: International Medical Devices, Inc. v. Cornell
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the plaintiff met its burden to show that asserted trade secrets were protectable under California law, and whether ideas that are generally known in an industry can constitute an inventive contribution for patent inventorship purposes.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the jury's finding of trade secret misappropriation, holding that the plaintiffs failed to establish that their asserted trade secrets regarding penile implant design and manufacturing were protectable because the information was generally known in the field. The court also reversed the patent inventorship correction, reasoning that contributions of generally known ideas cannot constitute inventive contributions.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies accused of trade secret misappropriation benefit from the court's rigorous scrutiny of whether asserted trade secrets are truly protectable, particularly where the information is arguably generally known in the industry.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret holders must ensure robust evidence that their claimed secrets are not generally known. The decision also limits the ability to correct patent inventorship based on contributions of commonly known concepts.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the PTO Director's instructions to the Patent Trial and Appeal Board governing discretionary denials of inter partes review institution constitute 'general statements of policy' exempt from APA notice-and-comment rulemaking requirements.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that the PTO Director's instructions guiding Board decisions on whether to institute IPR proceedings are general statements of policy exempt from notice-and-comment rulemaking under APA § 553(b). The court held these instructions do not bind the Director and relate to the exercise of unreviewable discretionary authority, defeating Apple's challenge to the PTO's IPR institution practices.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders benefit from the PTO retaining broad, judicially unreviewable discretion to decline IPR institution, reducing the risk that their patents will be subjected to post-grant challenges.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies and other frequent IPR petitioners face continued uncertainty about IPR institution practices, with no ability to challenge the Director's discretionary denial framework through APA rulemaking challenges.

impacts.caseName: Federal Express Corporation v. Qualcomm Incorporated
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Board erred in its obviousness determination of claims requiring 'reporting sensor information after a predetermined time delay,' and whether a non-party to district court litigation can file IPR petitions challenging patents asserted in that litigation on the filing deadline of the actual defendant.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the Board's finding that FedEx's sensor-based logistics patent claims were unpatentable as obvious and remanded for further proceedings. The case raised significant questions about whether third parties can file IPR petitions as surrogates for time-barred defendants, though the court declined to review the Board's denial of FedEx's termination motion on that basis.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders benefit from the vacatur of the obviousness finding and the court's scrutiny of third-party IPR petition filing practices that may be coordinated with time-barred defendants.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies relying on third-party IPR petitions to challenge patents asserted against them in litigation face uncertainty about the permissibility of such arrangements, potentially limiting a key defensive strategy.
